# ADR-0012 — Manifests are generated by the control plane, per quality class

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Supersedes:** nothing
**Related:** [ADR-0005](ADR-0005-cmaf-multi-drm.md) · [ADR-0008](ADR-0008-cdn-and-origin-abstraction.md) ·
[ADR-0011](ADR-0011-availability-projection-shape.md)

## Context

Two rules the platform already committed to turn out to collide.

**A resolution cap must be enforced server-side.** Licensors cap resolution by agreement, and plans
cap it commercially. `UsageRules::maxResolution` and `EntitlementSnapshot::maxResolution` have both
existed since Phase 2, and until now neither did anything: the playback response carried the cap as
a *restriction* the client was trusted to honour. The client is never a security boundary
([`CLAUDE.md`](../../../CLAUDE.md) §7), so a cap only a client enforces is not a cap.

**Cache offload is the dominant cost lever in delivery**
([`../../streaming/packaging-and-delivery.md`](../../streaming/packaging-and-delivery.md) §5). The
obvious way to enforce a cap — generate the manifest per viewer, listing only the renditions that
viewer may have — produces one cache entry per consumer. Offload collapses, origin egress rises by
roughly the ratio the cost model assumed, and nothing looks wrong until an invoice arrives.

There is also a question of *who* writes manifests at all. Most packagers emit both the segments and
the manifests that describe them. Delegating entirely would put the resolution cap inside a vendor
component, where it could not be tested, could not be reviewed as a contract change, and would have
to be re-implemented on every packager change.

## Decision

**Manifests are generated by the control plane, one per quality class, and the class is part of the
origin path.**

1. A small, **closed, append-only** set of quality classes — `h576`, `h720`, `h1080`, `h2160`,
   `full` — quantises every resolution cap. Quantisation always rounds **down**; an unrecognised
   cap is treated as the strictest class.
2. Publishing a channel generates a manifest for **every class × every format**, and writes them to
   the origin at `/{live|vod}/{uuid}/{class}/manifest.{m3u8,mpd}`.
3. Playback resolves the licensor's cap and the plan's cap, quantises, and hands Delivery the
   resulting class. Delivery addresses the corresponding manifest.
4. A capped viewer receives a manifest that **does not mention** the rungs they may not have.

The split with the packager is explicit:

| Artifact | Written by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| HLS multivariant playlist | **Us** | Entirely derived from ladder, packaging profile and quality class — all control-plane data |
| DASH MPD (live) | **Us** | `SegmentTemplate` with a fixed duration describes every segment by arithmetic; nothing needs appending as the packager publishes |
| HLS media playlists | **Packager** | Contents change with every segment emitted; only the packager knows what it has actually published |
| Segments, init segments | **Packager** | Media |

## Consequences

**The number of manifest variants per publication is the number of classes — five — not the number
of subscribers.** Every viewer sharing a cap shares a cached object. Segments are *not* duplicated
per class: the class decides which rungs a manifest mentions, never where their segments live, so
capped and uncapped viewers hit the same cached segments.

**Manifests become a reviewed artifact.** They are a client contract that behaves like one — a
change that looks harmless breaks a television that will never be updated, and the failure is
invisible in API tests, where status codes stay 200 while players stall. So generation is
byte-deterministic, golden-file tested, and a content hash is recorded per manifest, which makes a
republication that changed nothing distinguishable from one that did.

**A rendition ladder can no longer be changed without regenerating manifests.** Acceptable: it is
the same property that makes the change reviewable.

**Quantisation loses a little quality in the gaps.** A 900-line cap is served the 720 class. That is
the deliberate direction: serving one rung less than permitted costs picture quality, and serving one
rung more is a contract breach.

**A cap below the lowest rung still yields the lowest rung**, not an empty manifest. An empty
manifest is not a stricter outcome, it is a broken one — the viewer gets a player error instead of a
permitted, lower-quality stream, and the support contact costs more than the resolution difference.

**Adding a class is a migration, not a config change.** The set is append-only for the same reason
error codes and platform bitmask positions are: a stored manifest path must keep meaning what it
meant.

## Alternatives considered

**Per-viewer manifests.** Simplest enforcement, and it destroys cache offload. Rejected on cost.

**Cap enforced by the client from `restrictions`.** What the platform did before this ADR. The client
is never a security boundary, and a licensor asking how a cap is enforced cannot be answered with
"the app respects it".

**Cap enforced at the DRM licence instead.** Real, and it arrives in Phase 6 — licence policy derived
from usage rules is how HDCP and security level get enforced. It is not sufficient alone: it does
nothing for unencrypted content, and it fails *late*, after the player has already selected a
rendition it cannot play.

**Delegate all manifests to the packager.** Puts the cap inside a vendor component, untestable and
unreviewable, and re-implemented on every packager change. Rejected — but note the converse is also
rejected: we do **not** generate HLS media playlists, because we do not know what the packager
published.
